context.title: Capacity and achievement
context.text: A claim about what people can in principle understand does not mean that every person already knows it or learns without difficulty.
context.takeaway: Keep possibility distinct from present accomplishment.

context.text: Hall extends one philosophical account into several contested fields. Each extension needs its own reasoning and evidence.
context.takeaway: Agreement with the premise need not settle every application.

notice.text: Notice the step from an example to a universal claim.
notice.why: That step carries much of the argumentative burden.

notice.text: Follow qualifications about knowledge and resources.
notice.why: They prevent possibility from becoming a promise of effortless success.

opening: A brain evolved on one planet can explain stars it will never visit. Brett Hall takes that familiar achievement as evidence for a startling claim: human understanding has no fixed subject boundary. Building on David Deutsch's account of explanatory universality, he follows the implications into education, intelligence, and judgments about what other people can learn. The argument presses against the habit of treating present difficulty as a permanent limit, asking how much of what seems impossible is a problem for which the explanation has yet to be created.
